title: Sqrt(x)
description: Brute force to optimized: linear scan versus binary search on the answer, then Newton's method for even faster convergence.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a non-negative integer x, return the square root of x rounded down to the nearest integer, without using a built-in square root function.

blocks.text: Given a non-negative number x, return the square root of x, rounded down to the nearest whole number, without using a built-in square root function.

blocks.title: Analogy: Building the Biggest Square Garden Possible
blocks.text: Picture having exactly x square tiles and wanting to arrange as many of them as possible into a perfect square garden, with no gaps. If x is 8, the biggest perfect square you can build uses 4 tiles arranged 2 by 2, using 4 of the 8 tiles and leaving 4 unused, since a 3 by 3 garden would need 9 tiles, more than you have. The side length of the biggest square you can build, 2 in this case, is exactly the answer this problem is asking for.

blocks.caption: Find the largest whole number whose square does not exceed x

blocks.content: {"headers":["Candidate i","i squared","Fits within 8?","Why"],"rows":[["2","4","Yes","4 does not exceed 8, so 2 is still a valid candidate for the floor square root."],["3","9","No, too big","9 exceeds 8, so 3 is too large, confirming 2 is the largest valid candidate."]]}

blocks.text: The answer is 2, the largest i whose square does not exceed 8.
4 is a perfect square, 2 times 2 equals exactly 4, so the answer is simply 2 with no rounding needed.
The smallest possible input. The square root of 0 is 0.
Before writing any code, it helps to reason about what kind of condition this problem is really built on.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The question "is i squared at most x" is either true or false for any candidate i, and once it becomes false for some i, it stays false for every larger i, since squaring only grows as i grows.

Observation 2: That kind of condition, true for a run of small candidates then false forever after, is exactly the shape binary search is built for, even though there is no sorted array anywhere in sight here.

Observation 3: Binary searching directly over the range of possible answers, instead of scanning candidates one at a time, cuts the number of candidates checked from linear to logarithmic.

Observation 4: Going even further, Newton's method replaces the steady halving of binary search with a guess that gets pulled toward the true answer through repeated averaging, converging in even fewer steps.
That reasoning alone already reframes the whole problem: this is binary search on a range of answers, not a search through any array at all.
The most direct approach is to try every whole number starting from 0, squaring each one, until the square finally exceeds x. The last number that still fit is the answer.

items: Start i at 0.
While i squared is still less than or equal to x, increase i by 1.
Once the loop stops, i has gone one step too far, so return i minus 1.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: try every candidate one at a time, starting from 0

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The loop condition checks i times i against x, not i against the square root of x, specifically because the whole point is to avoid using a square root function at all, comparing squares instead of roots achieves the exact same result.
i is incremented until its square finally exceeds x, one step past the true answer, which is exactly why the final return steps back by one.
Starting i at 0 rather than 1 ensures x = 0 is handled correctly without any special case, since the loop simply never executes its body when x is 0.

blocks.text: This works because it checks every candidate in increasing order and stops the moment the square exceeds x, guaranteeing the last valid candidate is found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(square root of x), since the loop runs roughly that many times before the square exceeds x.
Space: O(1).

Limitation: checking every candidate one at a time wastes a lot of work for large x. The key property that makes this checkable much faster is that "i squared is at most x" is monotonic, once it becomes false for some i, it stays false for every larger i, which is exactly the condition binary search needs.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why checking every candidate works but is wasteful: most of the candidates checked are far from the true answer and could have been ruled out much earlier.

What makes the candidates skippable: the "is i squared at most x" condition is monotonic, true for every candidate up to the answer, false for every candidate after it.

Can a monotonic condition be searched faster than one at a time: yes, that is exactly the condition binary search is designed to exploit, by testing the middle candidate and discarding half the remaining range every time.

What are we binary searching over, if there is no array: the range of possible integer answers itself, from 1 up to a safe upper bound like x divided by 2.

The core idea: binary search directly over the candidate answers, using each midpoint's square as the comparison.

Instead of checking every candidate in order, binary search directly on the range of possible answers, from 1 up to x divided by 2 (a safe upper bound for any x of 4 or more). At each step, check the middle candidate: if its square is too big, the answer must be smaller, if too small, the answer must be bigger.

Binary search between 1 and x divided by 2. At each step, compare the midpoint's square to x, and narrow the search range accordingly. The search converges on the largest value whose square does not exceed x.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: binary search directly on the answer, using the squared-value comparison

blocks.text: This works because the condition "mid squared is at most x" is monotonic across the search range, exactly the property binary search requires: everything at or below the true answer satisfies it, everything above it does not. Each comparison of mid squared to x correctly determines which half of the remaining range still needs checking, and the search converges on hi landing exactly on the largest value whose square does not exceed x, once lo has moved past it.

items: The x < 2 special case is checked first specifically because the general binary search range, 1 up to x divided by 2, would incorrectly exclude 0 and 1 themselves as valid candidates.
hi starts at x divided by 2 rather than x itself, since for any x of 4 or more the true square root can never exceed half of x, a tighter, still always-safe starting bound.
Returning hi rather than lo at the very end is deliberate: by the time the loop exits, hi has landed on the largest candidate whose square did not exceed x, while lo has moved one step past it.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(log x), a genuine complexity class improvement over the linear scan.
Space: O(1).

Binary search is already fast, but there is a numerical method that converges to the square root even faster for large x: Newton's method. Starting from a guess, each new guess is the average of the current guess and x divided by the current guess, which pulls the guess toward the true square root far more aggressively than binary search's steady halving.

blocks.text: The guess converges to 2, matching the binary search result exactly.

blocks.caption: Further optimization: Newton's method converges by repeatedly averaging

items: The loop condition checks guess times guess against x, continuing to refine the guess only while it still overshoots, and stopping the instant it no longer does.
Each new guess averages the current guess with x divided by the current guess, the standard Newton's method update for finding a root of the function guess squared minus x.
Starting the initial guess at x itself is a simple, always-valid starting point, since x is guaranteed to already be at least as large as its own square root for any x of 1 or more.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(log log x) in practice for how quickly the guess converges once it gets close, since Newton's method roughly doubles the number of correct digits every step, faster than binary search's steady halving of the search range.
Space: O(1). For the small integer ranges typical in this exact problem the practical difference is minor, but the technique matters far more for high precision or very large number square roots.

blocks.text: The core pattern here is recognizing a monotonic condition ("is this candidate too big or too small") and using binary search to exploit it, rather than scanning every option one at a time. Newton's method is a good example of an even faster converging numerical technique worth knowing for problems that specifically care about numerical precision or very large inputs.

items: Using int multiplication for the midpoint's square without considering overflow for large x, a wider integer type avoids this.
Returning lo instead of hi at the end of the binary search, which off-by-one mistake gives an answer one too large.
Forgetting the x less than 2 special case, where 0 and 1 are already their own square roots.

blocks.text: This is one of the clearest examples of "binary search on the answer" rather than binary search on a sorted array, a pattern that shows up constantly once recognized. Mentioning Newton's method as a faster alternative, and explaining why it converges faster, signals awareness of numerical methods beyond typical discrete algorithms.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid checking every candidate", think: binary search directly over the range of possible answers, not over an array.
If the interviewer says "can this converge even faster", think: Newton's method, repeatedly averaging the guess with x divided by the guess.
If the interviewer says "why does binary search apply here, there is no array", think: binary search only needs a monotonic true or false condition over a range, not a sorted array specifically.

items: Why does binary search apply here even though there is no array to search over?

"Binary search on the answer" problems in general, where the search happens over a range of candidate answers rather than a sorted array, whenever a monotonic true or false condition exists.
Newton's method and other iterative numerical root-finding techniques, useful whenever high precision or very fast convergence matters more than exact integer arithmetic.
Any problem phrased as "find the largest or smallest value such that some condition holds," which is the general shape this problem's binary search is a specific instance of.
Overflow-aware arithmetic, since squaring a midpoint candidate can exceed a normal integer range, the same concern seen in other problems needing a wider intermediate type.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The linear scan runs in O(square root of x) time and O(1) space. Binary search brings that down to O(log x) time and O(1) space, a genuine complexity class improvement by exploiting the monotonic structure of the problem. Newton's method converges even faster in practice, though all three approaches use only O(1) extra space.

items: Pattern: binary search on the answer, exploiting a monotonic true or false condition over a range of candidates, with Newton's method as a faster converging numerical alternative.

Core Idea: "is this candidate's square at most x" is monotonic across the range of possible answers, so binary searching directly over that range finds the answer in logarithmic time, and Newton's method converges even faster by repeatedly averaging a guess toward the true root.
Time: O(square root of x) for the brute force, O(log x) for binary search, O(log log x) in practice for Newton's method.
Space: O(1) across every version.

Most Important Observation: binary search does not require a sorted array, only a monotonic condition over some ordered range of candidates, and recognizing that is what unlocks this entire "binary search on the answer" family of problems.
Interview Difficulty: easy to write the linear scan, but recognizing this as binary search on the answer, and knowing Newton's method as a further alternative, is what distinguishes a strong answer.
One line memory trick: binary search the answer space itself when the condition is monotonic, no array required.
